1.title: What JavaScript Is and Where It Runs
1.theory:
## What JavaScript is

JavaScript is a **programming language**. HTML is markup, CSS is styling, JS is **logic** — it makes sites interactive.

## Where it runs

- **In the browser** — Chrome, Firefox, Safari have engines (V8, SpiderMonkey).
- **On the server** — Node.js.
- **In mobile/desktop** — React Native, Electron (VS Code, Slack).

## How to connect to HTML

```html
<script>
  console.log("Hello");
</script>
```

Or via file: `<script src="script.js"></script>`.

Place `<script>` **at the end** of `<body>` so the DOM has time to build.

## JS is not HTML and not CSS

- HTML — **structure**
- CSS — **appearance**
- JS — **behavior**

If `<button>` is a button and `background: red` makes it red, then `button.addEventListener("click", ...)` is what happens on click.

## First program

```js
console.log("Hello, world!");
```

`console.log` — like `print` in Python or `System.out.println` in Java.

## What goes wrong

- Forgetting `;` — JS forgives (ASI), but better to use them.
- `<script>` before `<body>` — `querySelector` returns `null`.

## Common mistake

`<script>` in `<head>` without `defer` — runs before the DOM is built.

## Summary

- JS is a programming language
- Runs in browser and Node.js
- Connected via `<script>`
- `console.log` — output

questions.explanation: JS is a programming language. HTML — markup, CSS — styles.

practice.description:

```
Lesson 1
Done
```

2.title: Console, console.log
2.theory:
## Why console

Until we get to the DOM — all output goes to the **developer console**. F12 → Console. There: `console.log`, errors, warnings.

## console.log

```js
console.log("Hello");
console.log(42);
console.log(3 + 4);
```

Outputs `Hello`, `42`, `7`.

Accepts **any** number of arguments:

```js
console.log("Age:", 25);  // Age: 25
```

JS inserts a space between arguments.

## Quotes

`"Hello"`, `'Hello'`, `` `Hello` `` — equivalent. Template strings use backticks (lesson 6).

## Without quotes — variable

```js
console.log(Hello); // ReferenceError: Hello is not defined
```

## console.warn and console.error

```js
console.warn("warning");
console.error("error");
```

Output with markup.

## In browser vs Node.js

- Browser — F12 → Console.
- Node.js — terminal (`node script.js`).

Syntax is the same.

## What goes wrong

- `console.log()` without arguments — empty line.
- `console.log("a", "b")` — `a b`.

## Common mistake

`print("x")` from Python habit. In JS — `console.log`.

## Summary

- `console.log(...)` — output
- Any number of arguments
- `console.warn`, `console.error`
- Without quotes — variable access

questions.explanation: Hello is a variable, not defined — error.

```
Hello
```

3.title: Debugging in the Browser
3.theory:
## Why debugging

Code will break. **Debugging** — finding why. Without it, you're stuck staring at broken output.

## F12 → Console

Opens the developer tools. **Console** tab shows errors and `console.log` output. When something breaks — check here **first**.

## Reading errors

```
Uncaught ReferenceError: foo is not defined
    at script.js:5
```

- `ReferenceError` — error type
- `foo is not defined` — what went wrong
- `script.js:5` — file and line number

## Common error types

- **ReferenceError** — variable not defined
- **TypeError** — wrong type (calling a number as function, `null.foo`)
- **SyntaxError** — code structure is broken, nothing runs
- **RangeError** — number out of allowed range

## console.table / console.dir

```js
console.table([{a: 1}, {a: 2}]);   // pretty table
console.dir(obj);                   // expandable object
```

## Breakpoints

F12 → **Sources** tab → click on a line number. Code pauses there on next run. Hover over variables to see values. Step through with F10 / F11.

This is more powerful than `console.log` — you see everything at the pause point.

## debugger statement

```js
debugger;   // pauses here if DevTools is open
```

Cheap way to breakpoint.

## What goes wrong

- Ignoring the error message — 90% of the answer is there.
- `console.log` everywhere instead of a breakpoint.

## Common mistake

Guessing instead of reading. The browser tells you exactly what and where. Read it.

## Summary

- F12 → Console — read errors
- ReferenceError, TypeError, SyntaxError
- Breakpoints in Sources tab
- `debugger;` — pause inline
- Error message tells you where

questions.text: Where do you see JS errors in the browser?

4.title: let and const
4.theory:
## Two ways

`let` — variable. `const` — constant. `var` — **outdated**, don't use.

```js
let age = 25;
const PI = 3.14;
```

## let is mutable

```js
let x = 10;
x = 20;          // ok
console.log(x);  // 20
```

## const is not

```js
const y = 10;
y = 20;          // TypeError
```

## Rule

By default — `const`. Only when you change it — `let`.

## Why not var

`var` — old way with bugs:
1. **Function** scope (leaks out of `if`)
2. **Hoisting** (usable before declaration)

```js
if (true) { var a = 1; }
console.log(a); // 1 — leaked out

if (true) { let b = 1; }
console.log(b); // ReferenceError
```

## const and objects

`const` forbids **reassignment**, not content change:

```js
const obj = { a: 1 };
obj.a = 2;         // ok
obj = { b: 3 };    // TypeError
```

## Naming

camelCase: `userName`, `totalPrice`.

## What goes wrong

- `let x = 1; let x = 2;` — SyntaxError.
- `const x;` — SyntaxError, needs initialization.

## Common mistake

Habit of `var` from old tutorials.

## Summary

- `let` — mutable
- `const` — not
- `var` — outdated
- Default — `const`

5.title: Types and typeof
5.theory:
## Main types

| Type | Example |
|---|---|
| `number` | `42`, `3.14` |
| `string` | `"hello"` |
| `boolean` | `true`, `false` |
| `undefined` | "not set" |
| `null` | "empty" |
| `object` | `{}`, `[]` |

## number

All numbers — one type:

```js
console.log(typeof 42);     // number
console.log(typeof 3.14);   // number
```

## boolean

`true`/`false`, lowercase:

```js
console.log(typeof true);   // boolean
```

## undefined vs null

- `undefined` — variable with no value
- `null` — explicitly "empty"

```js
let x;
console.log(x);          // undefined

let y = null;
console.log(y);          // null
```

## typeof

```js
typeof 42          // "number"
typeof "hi"        // "string"
typeof true        // "boolean"
typeof undefined   // "undefined"
typeof null        // "object"  ← JS bug
typeof {}          // "object"
```

`typeof null` — `"object"`, historical bug.

## What goes wrong

- `typeof someVar` where `someVar` not declared — `"undefined"` (not an error).

## Common mistake

`True`/`False` capitalized. In JS only `true`/`false`.

## Summary

- `number`, `string`, `boolean`, `undefined`, `null`, `object`
- `typeof x` — type
- `typeof null` = `"object"`
- `undefined` — not set, `null` — explicitly empty

options: undefined — not set, null — explicitly empty

practice.description:


6.title: Strings
6.theory:
## Quotes

```js
"double"
'single'
`backtick`
```

Inside `"..."` you can use `'`, inside `'...'` you can use `"`.

## Template strings

Backticks + `${...}`:

```js
const name = "Anna";
const age = 25;
console.log(`Hi, ${name}! You are ${age}.`);
```

Inside `${}` — any expression: `` `${2 + 3}` `` → `5`.

## length

```js
console.log("Hello".length);   // 5
```

Property, not method.

## Methods

```js
s.toUpperCase()     // upper
s.toLowerCase()     // lower
s.trim()            // trim whitespace
s.includes("sub")   // contains
s.indexOf("sub")    // index or -1
s.slice(0, 3)       // from 0 to 3 (exclusive)
s.replace("a", "b") // replace
s.split(",")        // to array
```

Strings are immutable — methods return new:

```js
let s = "Java";
s.toUpperCase();
console.log(s);   // "Java"
```

## What goes wrong

- `s.length()` — error, `length` is a property.
- `s[0] = "X"` — silently no-op.

## Common mistake

`"a" + 5 + 6` → `"a56"`, not `"a11"`. Left to right.

## Summary

- Three quote types, backticks for interpolation
- `` `${expr}` ``
- `length` — property
- Methods return new string


7.title: Numbers
7.theory:
## One type number

`5` and `5.0` are one type. No `int`/`float`.

## Operators

```js
console.log(7 + 3);   // 10
console.log(7 - 3);   // 4
console.log(7 * 3);   // 21
console.log(7 / 3);   // 2.333...
console.log(7 % 3);   // 1
console.log(2 ** 10); // 1024
```

## Division by zero

```js
console.log(10 / 0);    // Infinity
console.log(0 / 0);     // NaN
```

## NaN

**Not a Number** — bad operation:

```js
console.log("abc" * 2);  // NaN
```

Check: `Number.isNaN(x)`.

## Math

```js
Math.round(3.7)    // 4
Math.floor(3.9)    // 3
Math.ceil(3.1)     // 4
Math.abs(-5)       // 5
Math.max(1, 5, 3)  // 5
Math.min(1, 5, 3)  // 1
Math.sqrt(16)      // 4
Math.random()      // 0 ≤ x < 1
```

## toFixed

```js
(3.14159).toFixed(2)   // "3.14" — string!
```

## Conversion

```js
Number("42")    // 42
Number("abc")   // NaN
parseInt("42")  // 42
parseFloat("3.14") // 3.14
```

## What goes wrong

- `0.1 + 0.2` → `0.30000000000000004` — floating point.
- `"5" - 3` → `2`, but `"5" + 3` → `"53"`.

## Common mistake

`toFixed` returns a string, not a number.

## Summary

- One `number`
- `Infinity`, `NaN`
- `Math.*`
- `toFixed(n)` — string
- `parseInt`, `parseFloat`, `Number`

practice.description:


- `Math.ceil(3.1)`
- `2 ** 10`

8.title: Type Coercion, == vs ===
8.theory:
## == vs ===

Two comparison operators:

- `==` — **loose**, with type coercion
- `===` — **strict**, no coercion

**Always use `===`.**

## Example

```js
console.log(5 == "5");    // true  — "5" became 5
console.log(5 === "5");   // false — different types
console.log(null == undefined);  // true
console.log(null === undefined); // false
```

`==` — source of weird bugs.

## `!=` and `!==`

Same: `!==` — strict "not equal".

## Explicit coercion

```js
Number("42")    // 42
Number("abc")   // NaN
String(42)      // "42"
Boolean(0)      // false
Boolean(1)      // true
Boolean("")     // false
Boolean("hi")   // true
```

## Truthy/falsy

In conditions **coerced to boolean**:

**Falsy**: `false`, `0`, `""`, `null`, `undefined`, `NaN`.

**Truthy** — everything else, including `"0"`, `[]`, `{}`.

```js
if ("") console.log("won't fire");
if ("0") console.log("fires — non-empty string");
if ([]) console.log("fires — empty array truthy");
```

## `+` and coercion

`+` is **string**, if any operand is string:

```js
console.log("5" + 3);   // "53"
console.log(5 + 3);     // 8
```

`- * /` — numeric, coerce:

```js
console.log("5" - 3);   // 2
console.log("5" * "2"); // 10
```

## What goes wrong

- `if (x == null)` — true for `null` and `undefined`.
- `if (x === null)` — only `null`.

## Common mistake

`if (x == 0)` — `""`, `false`, `0` all true. Strict `=== 0` only `0`.

## Summary

- `===` and `!==` — strict, always them
- `==` coerces — bug source
- `Number/String/Boolean` — explicit
- Falsy: `false`, `0`, `""`, `null`, `undefined`, `NaN`
- `+` string, `- * /` numeric

10.title: switch
10.theory:
## Syntax

```js
switch (day) {
  case 1:
    console.log("Mon");
    break;
  case 2:
    console.log("Tue");
    break;
  default:
    console.log("Other");
}
```

- `switch (value)` — any value
- `break` required, else **fall-through**
- `default` — if no case matched

## Fall-through

```js
switch (x) {
  case 1:
  case 2:
    console.log("1 or 2");
    break;
}
```

Empty cases group.

## switch vs if

`switch` — exact match. `if` — ranges.

## What goes wrong

- Forget `break` — falls into next `case`.
- No `default` and no match — nothing runs.

## Common mistake

Forget `break` — extra cases execute.

## Summary

- `switch (value) { case X: ... break; }`
- `break` — otherwise fall-through
- `default` — otherwise nothing
- Grouping: empty cases

13.title: Function Declaration
13.theory:
## Why functions

Break program into pieces: reuse, readability. One function — one task.

## Declaration

```js
function sum(a, b) {
  return a + b;
}

console.log(sum(2, 3)); // 5
```

- `function` — keyword
- `sum` — name
- `(a, b)` — parameters
- `return` — return value

## Call

`sum(2, 3)` — arguments. Order matters.

## Without return — undefined

```js
function f() {
  let x = 10;
}
console.log(f());  // undefined
```

## return ends function

```js
function check(x) {
  if (x > 0) return "plus";
  return "not plus";
  console.log("never");
}
```

## Parameters are copies

```js
function f(x) { x = 100; }
let a = 5;
f(a);
console.log(a);  // 5
```

Primitives by value. Objects/arrays by reference.

## What goes wrong

- Call before declaration — works, `function` is hoisted.
- Forget `return` — `undefined`.

## Common mistake

`function f() { return 5; }` — fine. `function f() { return 5 };` — `;` after `}` not needed.

## Summary

- `function name(params) { return ...; }`
- Without `return` — `undefined`
- `return` ends function
- Primitives — copies

14.title: Arrow Functions
14.theory:
## Function expression

Function as a value:

```js
const sum = function(a, b) {
  return a + b;
};
```

`sum` — variable holding a function.

## Arrow

Shorter:

```js
const sum = (a, b) => a + b;
console.log(sum(2, 3)); // 5
```

- `=>` instead of `function`
- One expression — implicit `return`
- One param — can drop `()`: `x => x * 2`

## With block

```js
const sum = (a, b) => {
  const result = a + b;
  return result;
};
```

`{}` present — `return` needed explicitly.

## No params

```js
const hi = () => console.log("hi");
```

## Difference from function

- No own `this` (matters in DOM, lesson 24)
- Can't use as constructor
- No hoisting — declare **before** use

## What goes wrong

- `const f = x => x * 2; f(3);` — 6.
- `const f = () => 5;` — returns 5.
- `const f = () => { 5 };` — `undefined` (no `return`).

## Common mistake

`() => { 5 }` — braces with expression, no `return` — returns `undefined`.

## Summary

- `(a, b) => a + b` — shorthand
- `() => { ...; return ...; }` — block
- One param — no `()`
- No hoisting

questions.text: What does `const f = x => x * 2; f(5)` return?
Can you call arrow before declaration?

15.title: Parameters and Rest
15.theory:
## Default values

```js
function greet(name = "guest") {
  return `Hello, ${name}!`;
}
console.log(greet("Anna"));  // Hello, Anna!
console.log(greet());        // Hello, guest!
```

## Rest (...)

Collect all arguments into array:

```js
function sumAll(...nums) {
  let total = 0;
  for (const n of nums) total += n;
  return total;
}
console.log(sumAll(1, 2, 3, 4));  // 10
```

`...nums` — array of all passed.

## Regular + rest

```js
function log(prefix, ...items) {
  console.log(prefix, ...items);
}
log("A", 1, 2, 3);  // A 1 2 3
```

`...items` — after regular.

## Spread

`...` in reverse:

```js
const arr = [1, 2, 3];
console.log(Math.max(...arr));  // 3
console.log([0, ...arr, 4]);    // [0, 1, 2, 3, 4]
```

## What goes wrong

- `function f(a, ...rest, b)` — SyntaxError, rest must be last.
- `greet(null)` — `null`, not default.

## Common mistake

`greet()` with `function greet(name)` — `undefined`, not empty string.

## Summary

- `param = default` — default
- `...rest` — all extras in array
- Rest — last
- Spread — expand array

questions.text: What does `function g(name = "guest") { return name; } g()` output?

17.title: Arrays
17.theory:
## What an array is

```js
const fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry"];
const nums = [3, 7, 1, 9, 4];
const empty = [];
```

## Indices

From 0: `arr[0]` — first, `arr[arr.length - 1]` — last.

```js
console.log(fruits[0]);  // apple
console.log(fruits[2]);  // cherry
console.log(fruits[-1]); // undefined — negatives don't work
```

## length

Property, not method:

```js
console.log(fruits.length);  // 3
```

## Mutation

Arrays are **mutable**:

```js
fruits[1] = "pear";
console.log(fruits);  // ["apple", "pear", "cherry"]
```

## Iteration

```js
for (const f of fruits) {
  console.log(f);
}
```

`for...of` — values.

```js
for (let i = 0; i < fruits.length; i++) {
  console.log(fruits[i]);
}
```

## Nested

```js
const matrix = [
  [1, 2, 3],
  [4, 5, 6]
];
console.log(matrix[1][2]); // 6
```

## What goes wrong

- `arr[10]` — `undefined`, not error.
- `arr.length = 2` — truncates array.

## Common mistake

`arr[-1]` — `undefined`, not last. For last — `arr[arr.length - 1]`.

## Summary

- `[a, b, c]` — array
- Indices from 0
- `length` — property
- `arr[i] = x` — mutation
- `for...of` — traversal

18.title: Array Methods
18.theory:
## push / pop

```js
arr.push(x)   // to end, returns new length
arr.pop()     // from end, returns removed
```

## shift / unshift

```js
arr.unshift(x)  // to start
arr.shift()     // from start
```

## slice — copy

```js
[1, 2, 3, 4].slice(1, 3)   // [2, 3]
[1, 2, 3, 4].slice(-2)     // [3, 4]
```

Doesn't mutate original.

## splice — mutate

```js
let arr = [1, 2, 3, 4];
arr.splice(1, 2);        // remove 2 from index 1 → [3, 4]
arr.splice(1, 0, 99);    // insert 99 at position 1
```

Mutates **in place**.

## includes / indexOf

```js
[1, 2, 3].includes(2)      // true
[1, 2, 3].indexOf(2)       // 1
[1, 2, 3].indexOf(99)      // -1
```

## forEach — iterate

```js
[1, 2, 3].forEach(n => console.log(n * 2));
// 2 4 6
```

## join

```js
[1, 2, 3].join("-")   // "1-2-3"
```

## reverse

```js
[1, 2, 3].reverse()   // [3, 2, 1] — mutates in place
```

## What goes wrong

- `push` returns new length, not array.
- `slice` — copy, `splice` — mutate.

## Common mistake

`arr = arr.push(x)` — `arr` becomes a number (new length). Just `arr.push(x)`.

## Summary

- `push/pop/shift/unshift` — ends
- `slice` — copy, `splice` — mutate
- `forEach` — iterate
- `join` — to string
- `reverse` — in place

19.title: map, filter, reduce
19.theory:
## map — transform each

```js
const nums = [1, 2, 3];
const doubled = nums.map(n => n * 2);
console.log(doubled); // [2, 4, 6]
```

Returns **new** array of same length.

## filter — keep matching

```js
const evens = nums.filter(n => n % 2 === 0);
console.log(evens); // [2]
```

Returns new array subset.

## reduce — to single value

```js
const sum = nums.reduce((acc, n) => acc + n, 0);
console.log(sum); // 6
```

`(acc, n) => ..., initial_value`.

- `acc` — accumulator
- `n` — current element
- `0` — start

## Example: sum

```js
[1, 2, 3, 4].reduce((acc, n) => acc + n, 0);  // 10
```

Step by step: 0 + 1 = 1, 1 + 2 = 3, 3 + 3 = 6, 6 + 4 = 10.

## Chaining

```js
const result = nums
  .filter(n => n > 1)
  .map(n => n * 10);
console.log(result); // [20, 30]
```

## What goes wrong

- Without initial value in `reduce` — first acc becomes `[0]`.
- `map` without `return` in arrow with `{}` — array of `undefined`.

## Common mistake

`map(n => { n * 2 })` — without `return` returns array of `undefined`. Either drop `{}`, or add `return`.

## Summary

- `map` — transform
- `filter` — keep
- `reduce` — fold
- Chains — JS power

20.title: Objects
20.theory:
## What an object is

`{ key: value }` — set of pairs. Like `dict` in Python.

```js
const user = {
  name: "Anna",
  age: 25,
  city: "Moscow"
};
```

## Access

Two ways:

```js
console.log(user.name);       // Anna
console.log(user["age"]);     // 25
```

Brackets — for dynamic keys.

## Modification

```js
user.age = 26;              // modify
user.email = "a@mail.com";  // add
delete user.city;           // delete
```

## in

```js
console.log("name" in user);  // true
console.log("email" in user); // false
```

## Object.keys / values / entries

```js
Object.keys(user)     // ["name", "age", "city"]
Object.values(user)   // ["Anna", 25, "Moscow"]
Object.entries(user)  // [["name", "Anna"], ...]
```

## Iteration

```js
for (const key in user) {
  console.log(key, user[key]);
}
```

`for...in` — keys.

## Nested

```js
const data = {
  user: { name: "Anna" },
  scores: [1, 2, 3]
};
console.log(data.user.name);  // Anna
console.log(data.scores[1]);  // 2
```

## What goes wrong

- `user.name` for missing — `undefined`.
- `user["age"]` — works, `user[age]` — tries to find variable `age`.

## Common mistake

`user.name` (dot) for key with space — only `user["first name"]`.

## Summary

- `{ k: v }` — object
- `obj.key` / `obj["key"]`
- `delete`, `in`
- `Object.keys/values/entries`
- `for...in` — keys

21.title: Destructuring
21.theory:
## Object destructuring

```js
const user = { name: "Anna", age: 25 };
const { name, age } = user;
console.log(name);   // Anna
console.log(age);    // 25
```

Pull fields into variables.

## Rename

```js
const { name: userName } = user;
console.log(userName);   // Anna
```

## Default

```js
const { name, city = "unknown" } = user;
console.log(city);   // unknown
```

## Array destructuring

```js
const [first, second] = [10, 20, 30];
console.log(first);   // 10
console.log(second);  // 20
```

## Skip elements

```js
const [, second] = [10, 20, 30];
console.log(second);  // 20
```

## Rest

```js
const [head, ...tail] = [1, 2, 3, 4];
console.log(head);  // 1
console.log(tail);  // [2, 3, 4]
```

## Function params

```js
function greet({ name, age }) {
  console.log(`${name}, ${age}`);
}
greet({ name: "Anna", age: 25 });
```

Common in React and modern code.

## Swap

```js
let a = 1, b = 2;
[a, b] = [b, a];
console.log(a, b);   // 2 1
```

## Nested

```js
const { user: { name } } = { user: { name: "Anna" } };
console.log(name);   // Anna
```

## What goes wrong

- `const { foo } = user` where no `foo` — `undefined`, not error.
- Accessing nested when parent missing — `TypeError`.

## Summary

- `const { a, b } = obj` — pull fields
- `{ a: newA }` — rename
- `{ a = 5 }` — default
- `[x, y] = arr` — array
- `[x, ...rest]` — rest
- Function params: `function f({ a, b })`

23.title: DOM, querySelector
23.theory:
## What DOM is

DOM — **Document Object Model**. Browser parses HTML into an object tree. JS reads and changes this tree.

`document` — root object.

## querySelector

Find **first** element by CSS selector:

```js
const title = document.querySelector("h1");
const byId = document.querySelector("#title");
const byClass = document.querySelector(".card");
```

Selectors like in CSS: `#id`, `.class`, `tag`, `[attr]`.

## querySelectorAll

Find **all**:

```js
const items = document.querySelectorAll("li");
console.log(items.length);
items.forEach(el => console.log(el.textContent));
```

Returns `NodeList` (array-like).

## If element not found

```js
const x = document.querySelector("#nope");
console.log(x); // null
```

Check for `null`.

## When DOM is available

`<script>` — after elements or with `defer`. Otherwise `querySelector` returns `null`.

## What goes wrong

- `querySelector(null)` — TypeError.
- Wrong selector — `null`.

## Common mistake

Script in `<head>` without `defer` — DOM not built yet.

## Summary

- DOM — object tree
- `querySelector` — first
- `querySelectorAll` — all
- CSS selectors
- Not found — `null`

25.title: Styles and Classes
25.theory:
## style

Direct CSS via JS:

```js
el.style.color = "red";
el.style.fontSize = "20px";
el.style.backgroundColor = "yellow";
```

In JS — camelCase: `background-color` → `backgroundColor`.

## classList

Work with classes:

```js
el.classList.add("active");
el.classList.remove("active");
el.classList.toggle("active");
el.classList.contains("active");
```

`classList` — better than `el.className` string.

## className

```js
el.className = "card active";  // overwrites all classes
```

Use `classList` to avoid wiping others.

## Style vs class

- `el.style.color = "red"` — **inline** style
- `classList.add("red")` + CSS `.red { color: red }` — via class

Class preferred — separates HTML and CSS.

## What goes wrong

- `el.style.background-color` — SyntaxError (hyphen). Use `backgroundColor`.
- `el.className = "new"` — wipes old classes.

## Common mistake

Hyphen in JS styles. Always camelCase.

## Summary

- `el.style.color = "..."` — inline
- `el.classList.add/remove/toggle` — via classes
- `classList` better than `className`
- In JS — camelCase

27.title: addEventListener, click
27.theory:
## What an event is

User clicked — **event**. JS can **listen** to events and react.

## addEventListener

```js
button.addEventListener("click", () => {
  console.log("clicked");
});
```

First arg — event type, second — handler.

## Common events

- `click` — click
- `submit` — form submit
- `input` — field input
- `keydown` — key press
- `mouseover` / `mouseout` — hover

## Multiple listeners

```js
btn.addEventListener("click", () => console.log("A"));
btn.addEventListener("click", () => console.log("B"));
```

Both fire.

## Removal

```js
function onClick() { console.log("once"); }
btn.addEventListener("click", onClick);
btn.removeEventListener("click", onClick);
```

Needs **same** function reference.

## onclick vs addEventListener

`el.onclick = fn` — works, but overwrites. `addEventListener` — multiple. Prefer `addEventListener`.

## What goes wrong

- Typo `"clikc"` — listener adds, never fires.
- `btn.addEventListener("click", alert)` — `alert` without `()` fires on click, `alert()` fires immediately.

## Common mistake

`addEventListener("click", fn())` — called immediately. Need `fn` without parens.

## Summary

- `addEventListener("click", fn)`
- `fn` without `()`
- Common: `click`, `submit`, `input`, `keydown`
- `removeEventListener` — same reference
- Prefer `addEventListener` over `onclick`

33.title: Promise
33.theory:
## What Promise is

Promise — object representing a **future value**. Three states:
- **pending** — waiting
- **fulfilled** — success (resolve)
- **rejected** — error (reject)

## Creation

```js
const p = new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
  setTimeout(() => resolve("done"), 1000);
});
```

## Usage

```js
p.then(result => console.log(result));  // "done"
p.catch(error => console.log(error));
```

## reject

```js
const p = new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
  reject(new Error("something broke"));
});
p.catch(err => console.log(err.message));
```

## Chains

```js
fetchData()
  .then(a => doSomething(a))
  .then(b => doAnother(b))
  .catch(err => console.log(err));
```

## Promise.all

All parallel, wait for all:

```js
Promise.all([p1, p2, p3]).then(results => {
  console.log(results);  // array of results
});
```

If any rejected — whole Promise.all rejected.

## Promise.race

First to finish:

```js
Promise.race([slow, fast]).then(result => console.log(result));
```

## Swallowing errors

`.catch` at end of chain catches any error above.

## What goes wrong

- Forget `.catch` — unhandled rejection.
- `resolve()` twice — second ignored.

## Common mistake

Confusing `Promise` with the function itself. `Promise` — returned value.

## Summary

- `new Promise((resolve, reject) => {})`
- `.then` — success, `.catch` — error
- `Promise.all` — all in parallel
- `Promise.race` — first
- Always add `.catch`

36.title: import / export
36.theory:
## Why modules

One file of 1000 lines — nightmare. Modules split code into files with clear boundaries.

## export

```js
// utils.js
export function add(a, b) {
  return a + b;
}
export const PI = 3.14;
export default function multiply(a, b) {
  return a * b;
}
```

- `export` — **named** exports (any number)
- `export default` — **one** default

## import

```js
// main.js
import { add, PI } from "./utils.js";
import multiply from "./utils.js";  // default
```

## Rename

```js
import { add as sum } from "./utils.js";
```

## import *

```js
import * as utils from "./utils.js";
console.log(utils.add(1, 2));
```

## In browser

`<script type="module" src="main.js"></script>` — `type="module"` required.

## In Node.js

- `.mjs` — module
- `.js` with `"type": "module"` in `package.json`

## Dynamic import

```js
const module = await import("./utils.js");
```

Lazy load.

## What goes wrong

- Forget `type="module"` — `import` won't work in browser.
- Typo in path — `Module not found`.
- Import named as default — `undefined`.

## Common mistake

Confuse named and default import. `import { add }` — for `export function add`. `import multiply` — for `export default`.

## Summary

- `export` — named
- `export default` — one
- `import { x }` / `import x`
- In browser — `type="module"`
- `as` — rename
